Isolation of Each Cell From Its Targets

Source: R/dp-isolation.R
dp_isolation.Rd

Usage

dp_isolation(
  resistance,
  radius,
  source_strength = NULL,
  destination = NULL,
  site_radius = NULL,
  source_threshold = 0.01,
  radius_units = c("pixels", "km"),
  resistance_is = "resistances",
  normalize = TRUE,
  n_draws = 64,
  seed = NULL,
  se = FALSE,
  contact = FALSE,
  progress = TRUE
)

Arguments

resistance

A terra::SpatRaster or file path: the resistance (or conductance) surface. Or a circuit from dp_circuit(), to reuse its factorization.

radius

Numeric. The dispersal radius: pairs of cells are counted if their centres are at most this far apart. In pixels by default (see radius_units). Inf counts all pairs.

source_strength

Optional terra::SpatRaster or file path on the same grid: target strength, e.g. habitat suitability. If NULL (default), the conductance surface is used, as in dp_omni(). With a destination, this is the origin strength: the targets of the destination_ layers.

destination

Optional terra::SpatRaster or file path on the same grid: destination strength, the targets of the origin_ layers. Default NULL: one set of targets.

site_radius

Numeric or NULL. The radius of the site each cell stands for (see "Sites"), in radius_units. 0 is the cell alone. Default NULL: 2 pixels, whatever radius_units.

source_threshold

Numeric. Cells with source (or destination) strength below this are not sources (or destinations). Default 0.01.

radius_units

Character. "pixels" (default): the radius counts cells, so the kernel is the cells with \(dr^2 + dc^2 \le\) radius\(^2\), as in os_run(). "km": great-circle distance between cell centres on lon/lat grids (the kernel narrows in degrees of longitude towards the poles), or distance in the coordinate reference system's units, converted to km, on projected grids.

resistance_is

Character. Whether resistance holds "resistances" (default) or "conductances". Ignored for a circuit.

normalize

Logical. Also compute flow potential and normalized current. Default TRUE.

n_draws

Integer. Number of draws (solves). Default 64.

seed

Integer or NULL. Seed for the random draws. If NULL (default), one is drawn from R's random number generator, so set.seed() also makes runs reproducible. The seed used is returned as the "seed" attribute.

se

Logical. Also return each layer's per-cell standard error, as layers with an _se suffix. Default FALSE.

contact

Logical. Also return each cell's contact resistance, the resistance of its own links in parallel, as the contact layer (see "Sites"). Default FALSE.

progress

Logical. Report progress through the 'progressr' package (see "Progress" in dp_omni()). Default TRUE; it shows only when a 'progressr' handler is active.

Value

A terra::SpatRaster with layers resistance and mean_resistance; with normalize, normalized_resistance and normalized_mean_resistance; and with se, an _se layer for each. With a destination, this set of layers twice, prefixed origin_ and destination_. With contact, a last layer contact. Attributes: "relative_se", each layer's median relative standard error over the cells with values, and "seed".

Details

Maps how well connected each cell is to its targets, as effective resistance: to the habitat within radius (source_strength), or, with a destination, between the two distributions in both directions. Where dp_omni() and dp_flux() map where movement passes, this maps how isolated each place is. Every cell with targets in reach gets a value, not only habitat, so it also shows how connected a site would be there.

A cell's targets are the other cells of its connected component within radius, each weighted by its share \(q_j\) of the cell's target strength in reach, \(A_i = \sum_{j \ne i} t_j k(d_{ij})\), where \(t\) is the target strength and \(k\) is 1 within radius and 0 otherwise. With \(R_{ij}\) the effective resistance between the sites around cells \(i\) and \(j\) (see "Sites") on the whole circuit, two layers summarise the targets:

resistance

Resistance to the target distribution: the effective resistance when one unit of current leaves the site and is withdrawn across its targets in proportion to \(q\). Many targets in reach act like parallel paths and lower it, so it measures how well the site is connected to its targets as a set. It is the injection of dp_flux() with the one site as the origin.

mean_resistance

Mean effective resistance to the targets, \(\sum_j q_j R_{ij}\): the difficulty of reaching a typical target. It is at least resistance, by the spread of the targets among themselves, and the targets that are hardest to reach weigh most in it. With site_radius = 0, summed over cells with weights \(w_i A_i\), it gives the total effective resistance over the pairs of dp_omni().

With a destination, each cell is scored in both directions, with origin_ and destination_ prefixes on the layers. The origin_ layers take the cell as an origin, with the destination (destination) as its targets: how well could movement from here reach the destination? The destination_ layers take the cell as a destination, with the origin (source_strength) as its targets: how reachable is this place from the origin? For present and future habitat, the first asks which populations can track their habitat, the second which future habitat can be colonised. Effective resistance is symmetric, so the two differ only in their targets.

Cells without targets in reach (none within radius in the same component) are NA. A cell is never its own target.

Sites

Each cell stands for a site: the cells within site_radius of it (2 pixels by default), across which the current is spread evenly. Targets are sites too, so \(R_{ij}\) above is the effective resistance between the sites around \(i\) and \(j\). This matters because on a grid, the effective resistance from a single cell grows only with the log of distance, so most of it is in the first few rings of links around the cell. A single cell's value is then dominated by its own contact resistance, the resistance of its own links in parallel, and maps the cell's own resistance more than its place in the landscape. Spreading the current over a site keeps that local term from dominating, as Circuitscape's focal regions do. Choose site_radius for the area a population or site occupies; values depend on it, so compare runs at the same site radius.

With site_radius = 0, each site is its single cell, and its own resistance is part of its isolation: the reading for a single point of interest. With contact = TRUE, the result includes the contact layer, each cell's contact resistance (exact, not estimated), which is a lower bound on the single-cell resistance. Subtracting it leaves the resistance beyond the cell's own links, but the subtraction doesn't remove any noise, so where contact is most of the value (high-resistance cells), the remainder is very noisy.

Method

Each draw injects a random-sign dipole across every link of the circuit, scaled by the square root of the link's conductance, and solves the circuit once. For the solution \(y\), \((y_i - y_j)^2\) is then an unbiased estimate of \(R_{ij}\) for every pair at once, and both layers come from sums of \(y\) and \(y^2\) over each cell's targets, after averaging \(y\) over each site. Their mean over draws estimates each layer without bias.

Flow potential has no direct analogue here. With normalize, the same draws on the uniform circuit (conductance 1 on the same cells) give the same quantities for geometry alone, and the normalized layers divide by them: the resistance of a unit-resistance landscape of the same shape that would give the same isolation, so in the units of the input's resistance. A normalized value of 2 means the cell is as isolated as it would be if every cell had resistance 2. Above the landscape's typical resistance, the cell is isolated by its resistances; below, by geometry (distance, edges, few targets) more than by resistance.

Accuracy

Each draw's estimate of resistance is a squared Gaussian-like quantity, so its relative standard error is about \(\sqrt{2 / \mathrm{n\_draws}}\) at any grid size: about 18% at the default 64 draws, and 10% at 200. mean_resistance averages over targets and is usually less noisy. Both circuits see the same draws, so on landscapes of modest contrast the noise of the normalized layers largely cancels, but where resistance varies by orders of magnitude it doesn't. With se = TRUE, the result includes each layer's per-cell standard error, from the spread of the draws; the "relative_se" attribute gives each layer's median relative standard error either way.

Reproducibility, performance and progress are as for dp_omni(): one factorization (two with normalize), then about n_draws solves.

See also

dp_omni(), dp_flux(), dp_circuit()

Examples

if (FALSE) { # circuitscaper::cs_julia_available(circuitscape = FALSE)
resistance <- terra::rast(system.file("extdata/resistance.tif",
                                      package = "circuitscaper"))
result <- dp_isolation(resistance, radius = 15, seed = 1)
terra::plot(result)
attr(result, "relative_se")

# Isolation between two distributions, in both directions
origin <- terra::rast(system.file("extdata/source.tif", package = "circuitscaper"))
destination <- terra::rast(system.file("extdata/ground.tif", package = "circuitscaper"))
between <- dp_isolation(resistance, radius = 45, source_strength = origin,
                        destination = destination, normalize = FALSE, seed = 1)
terra::plot(between)
DONTSHOW({JuliaConnectoR::stopJulia()})
}
